# Uppādavāra (Ya 2.2.1)

**ID:** Ya 2.2.1  
**Section:** Yamaka (ya)  
**Collection:** Abhidhamma  
**Title (Pali):** Uppādavāra  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/abh03m4.mul1.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/abh03m4.mul1.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Uppādavāra* ("Origination Section", Ya 2.2.1) forms the opening section of the *Pavattivāra* (process section) in the second chapter of the *Yamaka*, the sixth book of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka [Ronkin 2005]. Within the overarching framework of the *Yamaka*, doctrinal categories are methodically evaluated through a process division consisting of three successive cycles: origination (*uppādavāra*), cessation (*nirodhavāra*), and combined origination-cessation (*uppādanirodhavāra*) [Gal 2003; Ronkin 2005; Anderson 1999]. In this section, the analysis systematically examines the arising of phenomena across the three temporal periods (present, past, and future) according to analytical frames: with regard to person (*puggala*), realm or place (*okāsa*), and both person and place jointly (*puggalokāsa*), tested under both positive (*anuloma*) and negative (*paccanīka*) pairings [Nyanatiloka 2007].

Scholars note that the *Pavattivāra* analyses—beginning with the *Uppādavāra*—exemplify an early Buddhist process metaphysics, conceptualizing experience in terms of dynamic processes rather than enduring substances [Gal 2003; Ronkin 2005]. These sections are also doctrinally significant for documenting the early Abhidhamma development of momentary analysis (*khaṇa*), distinguishing specific sub-moments such as the origination-moment (*uppādakkhaṇa*) and dissolution-moment (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) [Gal 2003; Ronkin 2005].

**Sources**

- [Nyanatiloka 2007] Nyanatiloka Mahāthera, Guide Through the Abhidhamma Piṭaka (1938, repr. 2007) — Structural outline of the Uppādavāra across temporal modes, persons, and places in positive and negative formulations.
- [Ronkin 2005] Noa Ronkin, Early Buddhist Metaphysics (2005) — Analysis of the Yamaka process section (uppādavāra, nirodhavāra, uppādanirodhavāra), process metaphysics, and the development of sub-moments (uppādakkhaṇa).
- [Gal 2003] Noa Gal, Metaphysics of Experience. From the Buddha’s Teaching to the Abhidhamma (2003) — Discussion of the process section of Yamaka chapters and early momentariness.
- [Anderson 1999] Carol S. Anderson, Pain and Its Ending: The Four Noble Truths in the Theravāda Buddhist Canon (1999) — Division of the pavattivāra into uppādavāra, nirodhavāra, and uppādanirodhavāra across present, past, and future.
